parts.problem_md:
This question is about amino acids.

State the general formula for an amino acid.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The general formula for an α-amino acid is:
> 
> - RCH(NH<sub>2</sub>)COOH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You are expected to know the general formula for an α-amino acid.

parts.problem_md:
The amino acid alanine is shown in Fig. 1.1

![Structural formula of alanine](assets/001-structural-formula-of-alanine.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Draw the **two** structures of alanine in acidic and basic conditions.
parts.solution_md:
The structures of alanine in acidic and basic conditions are:

Acidic conditions:

![Structural formula of alanine in acidic conditions](assets/002-structural-formula-of-alanine-in-acidic-conditio.png)

Basic conditions:

![Structural formula of alanine in basic conditions](assets/003-structural-formula-of-alanine-in-basic-condition.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure alanine in acidic conditions
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structure alanine in basic conditions

> **[exam-tip]**
> Amino acids have both an acidic –COOH group and a basic –NH<sub>2</sub> group.
> 
> In acidic conditions (low pH), the –NH<sub>2</sub> group accepts a proton to give –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>. The –COOH group remains unchanged.
> 
> In basic conditions (high pH), the –COOH group loses a proton to give –COO<sup>–</sup>. The –NH<sub>2</sub> group remains unchanged.

parts.problem_md:
Electrophoresis is an analytical technique which separates ions by placing them in an electrical field.

Describe how a sample of amino acids can be separated using this technique.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A sample of amino acids can be separated using this technique by:
> 
> - A sample of amino acids is placed between two oppositely charged electrodes **[1 mark]**
> - The positively charged ions will move towards the negative electrode
> **AND**
> The negatively charged ions will move towards the positive electrode **[1 mark]**
> - Larger ions move more slowly
> **OR**
> Smaller ions move more quickly **[1 mark]**
> - Highly charged ions move more quickly
> **OR**
> Ions with a low charge move slowly **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question asks you to describe how amino acids are separated, not how they are identified.
> 
> After electrophoresis, an electropherogram is produced. This is a series of bands on the paper or gel, where each band corresponds to a particular species. The distance each band has moved from the origin indicates the relative size and charge of that species.

parts.problem_md:
A mixture of amino acids may be separated using electrophoresis. A typical practical set-up is shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Diagram of an electrophoresis apparatus](assets/004-diagram-of-an-electrophoresis-apparatus.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

When the power supply is switched on, some amino acids may not move, but remain stationary. Suggest an explanation for this observation.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Some amino acids remain stationary because:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark per point):
> 
> - The amino acid is uncharged / neutral / a zwitterion **OR** charges balance / are equal
> - It is equally attracted by the anode / + and the cathode / – **OR**
> It is attracted by neither the anode nor the cathode
> - The pH of the buffer is at the isoelectric point / IEP of the amino acid
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a sample of amino acids is placed between two oppositely charged electrodes:
> 
> - The positively charged amino acids will move toward the negative electrode
> - The negatively charged amino acids will move toward the positive electrode
> - Amino acids with an overall neutral charge will remain stationary
> 
> If the pH of the buffer is at the isoelectric point of the amino acid, neither the positively nor negatively charged ions will dominate and the amino acid will exist as a neutral zwitterion

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A mixture of amino acids may be separated using electrophoresis. A typical practical set-up is shown in Fig. 2.1.

When the power supply is switched on, some amino acids may not move, but remain stationary.

The amino acid glycine has the formula H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H. State the species formed on the filter paper if glycine moves to the left (positive) end of the filter paper.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The species formed is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub><sup>–</sup> / H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - If a species moves to the positive side, it must be negative
> - Glycine forms a negative ion by losing the H from the –COOH group

parts.problem_md:
The result shown in Fig. 2.2 was obtained from another electrophoresis.

![Electrophoresis result showing bands for three amino acid species A, B and C at different positions](assets/005-electrophoresis-result-showing-bands-for-three-a.png)

**Fig. 2.2**

What can be deduced about the relative sizes of, and charges on, the amino acid species **A**, **B** and **C**?

| **amino acid** | **relative size** | **charge** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** |   |   |
| **B** |   |   |
| **C** |   |   |
parts.solution_md:
The relative sizes and charges of **A**, **B** and **C** are:

| **amino acid** | **relative size** | **charge** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | **Final answer:** **small(est) / 1** | **Final answer:** **negative / –** |
| **B** | **Final answer:** **large(est) / 3** | **Final answer:** **negative / –** |
| **C** | **Final answer:** **middle / 2** | **Final answer:** **positive / +** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for **A **identified as the smallest **AND **negative
> 
> 1 mark for **B **identified as the largest **AND **negative
> 
> 1 mark for **C **identified as the middle / intermediate **AND **positive

> **[exam-tip]**
> The direction of travel depends on the charge on the ion:
> 
> - Species moving toward the positive side are negative
> - Species moving toward the negative side are positive
> 
> The distance the amino acid species travels depends on the size of the ion. Larger ions move more slowly
> 
> A has moved the furthest, so is the smallest species; B has moved the least, so is the largest species
> 
> You can use numbers to identify the relative sizes

parts.problem_md:

| **amino acid** | **structural formulae** |
|---|---|

| serine | H<sub>2</sub>NCH(CH<sub>2</sub>OH)CO<sub>2</sub>H |
| valine | H<sub>2</sub>NCH(CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>)CO<sub>2</sub>H |

i) State the number of different tripeptides that can be made using **one** molecule of **each** of the amino acids in Table 2.1.

[1]

ii) Draw the tripeptide, showing the peptide bonds in displayed form.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The number of different tripeptides that can be made using **one** molecule of **each** of the amino acids in Table 2.1 is:
> 
> - 6 / six **[1 mark]**

ii) An example tripeptide drawn showing peptide bonds in displayed form:

![Displayed structural formula of a tripeptide made from alanine, serine and valine showing peptide bonds](assets/006-displayed-structural-formula-of-a-tripeptide-mad.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for two displayed peptide bonds
> 
> 1 mark for the correct formula of the peptide

> **[exam-tip]**
> The three amino acids can be arranged in six different ways:
> 
> - alanine-serine-valine
> - alanine-valine-serine
> - serine-alanine-valine
> - serine-valine-alanine
> - valine-alanine-serine
> - valine-serine-alanine
> 
> You would get credit for any one of these tripeptides, so the central R groups of each amino acid can be shown in any order
> 
> You can write this as a structural formula but with the peptide bond, –NHCO– shown in displayed form

parts.problem_md:
Much research has been carried out in recent years investigating the exact structure of silk. The silk of a spider's web is at least five times as strong as steel, and twice as elastic as nylon. The silk fibre is composed of many identical protein chains, which are mainly made from the amino acids glycine, alanine and serine, shown in Fig. 1.1, with smaller amounts of four other amino acids.

![Structural formulae of glycine, alanine and serine](assets/007-structural-formulae-of-glycine-alanine-and-serin.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Amino acids can exist as zwitterions. Draw the zwitterion structure for glycine.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The zwitterion structure of glycine is:
> 
> - NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When an amino acid forms a zwitterion, the hydrogen ion from the –COOH group is transferred to the –NH<sub>2</sub> group. This produces a molecule with both a positive charge (on the nitrogen) and a negative charge (on the oxygen), but with no overall charge.
> 
> To draw the zwitterion of glycine: move the H from –COOH to –NH<sub>2</sub>, add a positive charge to give –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, and add a negative charge to give –COO<sup>–</sup>.
> 
> Do not show individual single bonds in the structural formula.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Much research has been carried out in recent years investigating the exact structure of silk. The silk of a spider's web is at least five times as strong as steel, and twice as elastic as nylon. The silk fibre is composed of many identical protein chains, which are mainly made from the amino acids glycine, alanine and serine, shown in Fig. 1.1, with smaller amounts of four other amino acids.

![Structural formulae of glycine, alanine and serine](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/03/xLItzEXi_glycine-alanine-serine.png)

{align=center} **Fig. 1.1**

Amino acids can act as acids or bases. Construct equations to show:

i) the reaction between alanine and HCl (aq),

[1]

ii) the reaction between serine and NaOH (aq).

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction between alanine and HCl (aq) is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>NCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)COOH + HCl → <sup>+</sup>H<sub>3</sub>NCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)COOH + Cl<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction between serine and NaOH (aq) is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>NCH(CH<sub>2</sub>OH)COOH + NaOH → H<sub>2</sub>NCH(CH<sub>2</sub>OH)COONa + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Amino acids exist as zwitterions in solution. Think of the amino acid as having two separate functional groups: an acidic –COOH group and a basic –NH<sub>2</sub> group.
> 
> When HCl is added, the H<sup>+</sup> ion protonates the –NH<sub>2</sub> group to give –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>. The –COOH group remains unchanged.
> 
> When NaOH is added, the OH<sup>–</sup> ion deprotonates the –COOH group to give –COO<sup>–</sup>, with the Na<sup>+</sup> forming the sodium salt. Water is produced.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Much research has been carried out in recent years investigating the exact structure of silk. The silk fibre is composed of many identical protein chains, which are mainly made from the amino acids glycine, alanine and serine, shown in Fig. 1.1, with smaller amounts of four other amino acids.

i) Draw the structural formula of a portion of the silk protein, showing three amino acid residues. Label a peptide bond on your structure.

[3]

ii) State the polymer **type** of silk protein.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) The structural formula of a portion of the silk protein, with a peptide bond labelled, is:

![Structural formula of a silk protein chain showing three amino acid residues connected by peptide bonds](assets/008-structural-formula-of-a-silk-protein-chain-showi.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct CO–NH bonding, including at least one C=O bond
> 
> 1 mark for at least one peptide bond labelled
> 
> 1 mark for 3 amino acid residues shown

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The polymer **type** of silk protein is:
> 
> - Condensation
> **OR**
> Polyamide **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The amine group of one amino acid reacts with the carboxylic acid group of the next. A water molecule is lost (condensation reaction) and a peptide bond (C(=O)–NH) forms between them.
> 
> The structural formula you draw must contain 3 residues. A residue is an amino acid that has lost a water molecule when forming the chain. The three residues do not all need to be different, but should be glycine, alanine or serine.
> 
> A polyamide is a condensation polymer containing amide (peptide) bonds. Silk and nylon are both polyamides.

parts.problem_md:
The *M*<sub>r</sub> of a silk protein molecule is about 600,000. Assuming it is made from equal amounts of the three amino acids in Fig. 1.1, calculate the average number of amino acid residues in the protein chain. Show your working.

[*M*<sub>r</sub> (glycine) = 75;   *M*<sub>r</sub> (alanine) = 89;     *M*<sub>r</sub> (serine) = 105]

number of residues .............................................
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the average number of amino acid residues in the protein chain:

- List the known values:

  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(glycine) = 75
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(alanine) = 89
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(serine) = 105
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(protein chain) = 600 000
- Determine the *M*<sub>r</sub> of one repeating unit of three amino acid residues (each residue loses one water molecule when forming the chain):

(75 − 18) + (89 − 18) + (105 − 18)

= 57 + 71 + 87 = 215

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the number of three-residue sets in the protein chain:

$\frac{600000}{215}$

= 2791

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the total number of amino acid residues:

2791 x 3 = **8372**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for calculating the *M*<sub>r</sub> of one repeating unit of three amino acid residues: 215
> 
> 1 mark for calculating the number of three-residue sets in the protein chain: 2791
> 
> 1 mark for calculating the total number of amino acid residues: 8372

> **[exam-tip]**
> When an amino acid joins a protein chain via a peptide bond, one water molecule (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 18) is lost per residue. Subtract 18 from each amino acid *M*<sub>r</sub> to find the residue *M*<sub>r</sub>.
> 
> The second step gives the number of repeating three-residue sets. Multiply by 3 to get the total number of individual amino acid residues.
> 
> If you did not subtract 18 from each *M*<sub>r</sub> value (using 75 + 89 + 105 = 269 instead of 215), you would still score 2 marks if the method for steps 2 and 3 is correct.

parts.problem_md:
The amino acid alanine is shown below.

![Structural formula of alanine](assets/009-structural-formula-of-alanine.png)

Alanine will react with excess chloromethane. Draw the structural formula of the product formed in this reaction.
parts.solution_md:
The structural formula of the product formed in the reaction between alanine and excess chloromethane:

![Product of alanine reacting with excess chloromethane](assets/010-product-of-alanine-reacting-with-excess-chlorome.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure with a positive charge on the main compound **AND** a chloride / Cl<sup>–</sup> counter-ion

> **[exam-tip]**
> The lone pair on the nitrogen atom allows it to act as a nucleophile. Amino acids react with halogenoalkanes in a similar way to amines
> 
> Further substitution of the hydrogen atoms forms a secondary and then tertiary amine, and finally a quaternary ammonium salt
> 
> The clue is that the halogenoalkane is in excess. So, the available lone pair on the nitrogen can attack a δ+ carbon on another chloromethane molecule
> 
> This question is often answered incorrectly. The amine produced is actually more reactive due to the lone pair on the nitrogen being more readily available

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The amino acid alanine is shown below.

i) Explain why alanine has a high melting point compared with amines of similar molecular mass.

[2]

ii) Draw the structural formula of alanine in the solid state.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Alanine has a high melting point because:
> 
> - Alanine exists as a zwitterion / ionic form in the solid state **[1 mark]**
> - The zwitterions form an ionic lattice / strong electrostatic forces exist between them, requiring more energy to break **[1 mark]**

ii) The structural formula of alanine in the solid state:

![Displayed structural formula of alanine as a zwitterion](assets/014-displayed-structural-formula-of-alanine-as-a-zwi.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A zwitterion is a compound with no overall electrical charge, but which contains separate parts that are positively and negatively charged
> 
> The structure of an amino acid allows it to act as both an acid and a base. At the isoelectric point, nearly all amino acid molecules exist as zwitterions
> 
> Amino acids adopt the zwitterionic form in the solid state, forming an ionic lattice similar to ionic compounds

parts.problem_md:
The isoelectric point is the pH at which an amino acid exists as a zwitterion. The isoelectric point of valine is 6.0 and of lysine is 9.8 and their structures are shown below.

valine                                                           lysine

![Displayed structural formulae of valine and lysine](assets/015-displayed-structural-formulae-of-valine-and-lysi.jpeg)

![Electrophoresis apparatus diagram](assets/016-electrophoresis-apparatus-diagram.png)

A mixture of the dipeptide, val-lys, and its two constituent amino acids, valine and lysine, was analysed by electrophoresis using a buffer at pH 6.0.

Draw and label **three** spots on the diagram in Fig. 1.1 of the electrophoresis paper to indicate the likely position of each of these species after electrophoresis. Explain your answer.

![Blank electrophoresis result showing starting position](assets/017-blank-electrophoresis-result-showing-starting-po.png)

**Fig. 1.1**
parts.solution_md:
The labelled electrophoresis paper is:

![Annotated electrophoresis result showing valine at origin and val-lys and lysine to the right](assets/018-annotated-electrophoresis-result-showing-valine-.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for valine on the cross
> 
> 1 mark for Val-Lys and Lys on the right of the cross (in any order)
> 
> 1 mark for the relative order of Val-Lys and Lys (on the same side of the cross)
> 
> Explanation of movement:
> 
> - Val does not move as it is a zwitterion / neutral (at pH 6) **OR**
> Lys / Val-Lys move towards the negative pole as they are positively charged **[1 mark]**
> - Lys moves the furthest as it has the lowest *M*<sub>r</sub> (with the same positive charge) **OR**
> Val-Lys moves the least as it has the largest *M*<sub>r</sub> (with the same positive charge) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The isoelectric point is the pH at which an amino acid exists as a zwitterion, which means that the overall charge depends on the pH of the buffer solution
> 
> Val will exist as a zwitterion as the buffer pH (6.0) equals its isoelectric point
> 
> Lysine and val-lys will have a positive charge overall as the basic side chain amine group is protonated to form –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> at pH 6.0
> 
> Lysine and val-lys have the same overall charge at pH 6 as both contain two NH<sub>2</sub> groups that are protonated (one on the side chain, one on the terminal amine)
> 
> The larger the *M*<sub>r</sub>, the less the amino acid or dipeptide will trave, which explains why valine, lysine, and val-lys can be separated

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Tryptophan is a naturally occurring α-amino acid. Its structure is shown below.

Deduce the molecular formula for tryptophan and write a balanced equation for the reaction of tryptophan with dilute nitric acid.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The molecular formula and equation are:
> 
> - Molecular formula: C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>12</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Equation: C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>12</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N<sub>3</sub>O<sub>5</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When an amino group reacts with a dilute acid it is protonated:
> 
> RNH<sub>2</sub> + H<sup>+</sup> → RNH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>
> 
> Tryptophan has only one basic amino group, which is the α-amino group (–NH<sub>2</sub>) attached to the central carbon
> 
> The nitrogen in the indole ring is part of the aromatic π system; its lone pair is delocalised into the ring and cannot be protonated by dilute acid
> 
> Adding one mole of HNO<sub>3</sub> contributes 1H, 1N, and 3O to the molecular formula of tryptophan, giving the ammonium nitrate salt C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N<sub>3</sub>O<sub>5</sub>

ii) The species formed when alanine is in a solution of high pH:

![Structural formula of alanine in basic conditions showing the deprotonated carboxylate form](assets/025-structural-formula-of-alanine-in-basic-condition.png)

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The isoelectric point is:
>

ii) The structure of alanine at pH 6.0:

![Structural formula of alanine as a zwitterion at pH 6.0](assets/027-structural-formula-of-alanine-as-a-zwitterion-at.png)

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Fig. 3.1 shows the structures of the amino acids, alanine and valine.

Valine exists as a pair of stereoisomers.

State what is meant by the term stereoisomers and how the stereoisomers of valine can be distinguished from one another.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Stereoisomers are defined as follows:
> 
> - Molecules with the same structure / structural formula **[1 mark]**
> - But with bonds / atoms / groups arranged differently in space **[1 mark]**
> 
> The stereoisomers of valine can be distinguished by:
> 
> - Plane polarised light **[1 mark]**
> - Will be rotated equally in opposite directions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Amino acids that have four different groups bonded to a carbon atom exhibit optical stereoisomerism
> - A pair of enantiomers exist which are mirror images of one another
> - A solution of one enantiomer rotates the plane of polarisation in a clockwise direction; the other rotates it anti-clockwise by the same angle
> - When optically active substances are made in the lab, they often occur as a 50/50 mixture of the two enantiomers — this is known as a racemic mixture or racemate
